# MAXGEN — The Maxwell Genealogy Standard (v2.1) — full text of opengenealogyai.org



---
## MAXGEN

An open standard · public domain · current release v2.1
Genealogy data that is honest about what it doesn't know.
MAXGEN is a free, open data standard for family history. Every fact carries its source and a confidence score. Conflicting evidence is kept, not deleted. Anyone can use it, build on it, or extend it. No permission required.

ReadWhat the standard is and why it exists
ListenEight podcast episodes, recorded for v1.11
DownloadThe twelve schema files, every version





## The problem it solves

Genealogy has never had more to work with. Close to two billion records are online, archives scan more every year, volunteers transcribe registers by the million, and DNA testing has added a whole new kind of evidence. The formats we exchange that work in were designed for a simpler time: one birth year, one birthplace, one set of parents, written down as settled fact. Real family history rarely arrives that clean. A census says 1843; a gravestone says 1844. A father could be one of three men with the same name.

MAXGEN writes the doubt down. It stores **what the document says** separately from **what we think it means**, keeps every claim with its source and a 0-to-1 confidence score, and never overwrites anything. Several possible parents can coexist until the evidence resolves them. Every uncertainty becomes a lead worth chasing instead of a dead end, and as each new source corroborates a name or a date you watch the evidence for it grow. People can read it, researchers can check it, and AI can work with it without inventing anything, because confidence is a machine's native language.

MAXGEN is built to sit alongside the archives, record sites, and communities researchers already rely on, not to replace them. It is a shared language they can all speak. Every ancestor. Every source. Every honest doubt.

## The eleven record schemas

A schema is a written rule-set that says exactly what fields a record has and what each one means, so that any program can read a record written by any other program. Since version 2.0, MAXGEN has eleven record schemas, plus one shared file of building blocks that they all use, and each record schema has its own page.



## Three promises

1. **Nothing is ever deleted.** A retracted claim gets a retraction note; it does not vanish. The audit trail is permanent.
2. **Living people are protected by the schema itself.** A record about a person who may be alive is locked private no matter what any application does.
3. **Records stay valid within a major version.** Within 2.x every change is additive: fields are never renamed or removed, and a file valid under 2.0 stays valid under every 2.x release. See the [changelog](/changelog/).

## Who it is for

- **Developers** building genealogy tools or AI agents: twelve JSON Schema files (eleven record schemas and one shared file) at stable addresses, a changelog, made-up examples, and a [validator](/validator/) that runs in your browser.
- **Genealogists and archivists** deciding whether to trust it: the [plain-English guide](/standard/), the [FAQ](/faq/), and the [podcasts](/podcasts/).
- **Institutions** who need to know how it is governed before adopting it: the [governance page](/governance/) and the [licence](/license/).

MAXGEN is short for the Maxwell Genealogy Standard, named for its author, Garlon Maxwell. It is stewarded by OpenGenealogyAI and dedicated to the public domain (CC0).


---
## The Standard

The Maxwell Genealogy Standard · v2.1 · CC0
# The Standard

MAXGEN is a language for describing family-history evidence. It is not a product, not a database, and not a website. It is a set of eleven record schemas (written rule-sets for data records), plus one shared file of building blocks, that any program can read and write, so that research done in one place can be understood everywhere else. This page explains the standard in plain English. The exact rules live in the [schema files](/schemas/).

## 1. What is MAXGEN?

MAXGEN is an open JSON standard for representing genealogical evidence and the people it describes in a way that is **honest about uncertainty**.

Some or most genealogy formats today can hold one answer per fact. When two records disagree about who someone's father was, one has to win and the other is set aside. MAXGEN takes a different approach: **every fact is a claim** that cites its evidence and carries a confidence score. Nothing is overwritten. Several possible parents can coexist. Conflicting birth years both survive. The uncertainty is the data.

Five ideas define it:

1. **Uncertainty is data.** Every claim carries a 0-to-1 confidence score (section 6). A date keeps the document's own words plus what they mean (about, before, between, worked out from an age), and its earliest and latest possible days are worked out whenever it is read, because a census age is a guess and "spring 1847" is not a day.
2. **Evidence and interpretation are kept apart.** MaxRecord holds what a document says, exactly as written. MaxPerson and MaxRelationship hold what we think it means: who the people were and how they were related. You can change your mind about a person without touching the document.
3. **Nothing is ever deleted.** A wrong claim is retracted with a reason and stays visible as withdrawn, and a wrong merge can be undone. A contested claim is marked `disputed`, not removed. Every claim names the task that produced it, and every task records who did the work.
4. **Privacy is built into the schema.** Every document that names a person must say whether that person may be alive, and when unsure the answer is yes. Anything about a person who may be alive is locked to the most restrictive licence, `tier2-private`, and privacy is worked out again whenever the data is read, never from a stored copy. DNA records are always private and never hold raw genetic data.
5. **Extensions are the escape hatch.** Each schema is closed, so validation is exact, but every schema has an `extensions{}` object that accepts anything. You never need to fork.

> **The core principle:** a claim with low confidence and a real source is worth more than a certain-looking answer with no source. MAXGEN never invents. When the document is unclear, the confidence score says so.

## 2. How MAXGEN differs from GEDCOM

GEDCOM is the 1984 file format that most genealogy programs can import and export. It is one of the great successes of the field: forty years of trees have moved between programs because of it, and GEDCOM 7 continues to modernise it. MAXGEN is not a replacement for exchanging finished trees. It is a companion for exchanging the **evidence and reasoning** behind a tree, a job GEDCOM was never asked to do. The two are meant to work together.

| | GEDCOM | MAXGEN |
|---|---|---|
| Format | Custom plain text (`.ged`) | JSON, validated by JSON Schema |
| Relationships | A child can be linked to more than one family, with a pedigree type (`PEDI`) | Every family link stored once, in MaxRelationship; a child can belong to several parent sets (birth, adoptive, step, foster and more), and a competing candidate is kept until a written proof settles it |
| Uncertainty | A quality rating on a citation (`QUAY`) | The point of the design: a confidence on every claim |
| Source for each fact | Optional | Required on every claim: exactly one piece of evidence |
| Dates | A date value, with an optional phrase (`PHRASE`) | The words as written, plus what they mean (about, before, between, worked out from an age); earliest and latest days are worked out when read |
| Conflicts | A child's family link can be marked challenged or disproven (`STAT`) | Competing claims are kept side by side, and each claim's status says where it stands (proposed, proven, disputed, disproven, retracted) |
| Living people | A restriction marker (`RESN`) | Every document that names a person must say whether they may be alive; if so, the schema locks it private |
| Transcription provenance | None | MaxRecognition, down to word-level confidence; on a MaxRecord, the chain of copies back to the original |
| Name variants across languages | Translations of a name (`TRAN`) | MaxName: variants and cross-language cognates, each citing evidence |
| AI readiness | Predates it | Structured evidence on every claim, quotes checked against the document's words, and a `fabricated_or_hallucinated` rejection reason for reviews in MaxTask |
| Control | A steering committee | Public domain (CC0); anyone may use, fork, or extend |

The MAXGEN 2.0 specification gives every GEDCOM 7 construct a home, so a GEDCOM import need not lose anything on the way in: `CENS`, `EMIG`, `IMMI`, `NATU`, `PROB` and `WILL` become events of the matching type, `RESI` and `OCCU` become residence and occupation facts, and a tag with no field of its own is kept word for word in `extensions`. It maps GEDCOM X, Gramps and RootsMagic the same way. The importers that follow this mapping are not published yet.

## 3. The eleven record schemas

A schema is a written rule-set that says exactly what fields a record has and what each one means. MAXGEN began with three record types, grew to seven during the 1.x releases, and in 2.0 has eleven record schemas plus one shared building-blocks file, each covering one layer of the research process. Each record schema has [its own page](/schemas/).

| Schema | What one document is | Page |
|---|---|---|
| **MaxRecord** | One document, copied word for word | [MaxRecord](/schemas/maxrecord/) |
| **MaxPerson** | One person, as a researched conclusion (holds no family links) | [MaxPerson](/schemas/maxperson/) |
| **MaxRelationship** | One family link, stored once: a `family`, a `parent_child` pair or an `association` | [MaxRelationship](/schemas/maxrelationship/) |
| **MaxTask** | One piece of work: research, an import, a review or a proof | [MaxTask](/schemas/maxtask/) |
| **MaxSource** | One work, collection or repository | [MaxSource](/schemas/maxsource/) |
| **MaxPlace** | One real place with its history | [MaxPlace](/schemas/maxplace/) |
| **MaxGroup** | One historical group (its own facts only; no member list) | [MaxGroup](/schemas/maxgroup/) |
| **MaxEvent** | The identity of one occasion (thin) | [MaxEvent](/schemas/maxevent/) |
| **MaxName** | Knowledge about one name | [MaxName](/schemas/maxname/) |
| **MaxRecognition** | One machine reading of an image | [MaxRecognition](/schemas/maxrecognition/) |
| **MaxDNA** | One person's DNA test and its matches (always private) | [MaxDNA](/schemas/maxdna/) |

The twelfth file, `maxgen-defs.schema.json`, is not a record type: no document is valid against it. It holds the parts every record schema uses: ids and small types, the date block, the place block, the evidence link (the part of every claim that says which evidence it rests on), the quote check, saved copies, regions and media pointers, roles and event types, the claim header, the common and lifecycle fields, and the task provenance block.

How they fit together:

```
                             MaxSource
                (a work, collection or repository)
                                 ▲
                                 │ part of
                                 │
  MaxRecognition ──reads───► MaxRecord ◄──── cited as evidence by claims
  (a machine reading         (one document,
   of its image)              copied word for word)

  MaxRelationship ──links──► MaxPerson ──claims point at──► MaxPlace  (one real place)
  (every family link,        (one person, as a              MaxGroup  (one historical group)
   stored once)               researched conclusion)        MaxEvent  (one occasion)
                                 ▲
                                 │ took the test
                                 │
                              MaxDNA (one person's test and matches, always private)

  MaxName   knowledge about one name: its variants and cognates
  MaxTask   the work behind every claim: proofs and search steps live here
```

Every claim, in every schema, cites exactly one piece of evidence: a document (a MaxRecord), an imported tree file, DNA matches, an accepted proof, or a recorded search. Every claim also names the MaxTask that produced it.

A MaxRecord needs no other document to be valid, only the shared file every schema uses, so an archive that only wants to publish its documents, copied word for word, can start with MaxRecord alone.

Sections 4 to 7 are the rules that MAXGEN's reference agent kit follows, copied word for word from its `RULES.md`. Where they mention "the kit", "the helper", the Orchestrator or the person's page, they mean that kit.

## 4. Who decides

**The kit cannot tell who is typing.** A decision counts as the person's own only when the
person makes it on their Probable Pedigree page (`probable_pedigree.py`). An answer the
Orchestrator types for them (`task ... --answer`) is recorded as relayed. A relayed answer is
enough for a merge, an adoption, lowering a living flag, and for "disputed" or "disproven".
**"Proven" needs the person's own decision on their page.** So the person-page address is for
the person's own hands: an agent never opens it, fetches it with a program or presses its
buttons, and never reuses it after giving it to the person.

**The person's own choices are theirs alone (R-33, R-34).** Who is held back from sharing, what
is shared, which people are locked, and their bookmarks, tags and saved lists live in the tree's
owner tables. Only the person changes them, in their own Probable Pedigree, which holds the
tree's owner key; you never ask for that key, never look for it and never write those tables.
Never change a person the owner has locked, nor a family link of theirs: the helper refuses it
(R-34). If a locked person needs a change, tell the person through the Orchestrator and let
them unlock it. The one thing you may record there is how many records a website holds for a
person (an `outside_holdings` mark), because that is a finding, not a choice.

**The person may withdraw anything, and bring anything back (R-35).** When the person withdraws
something you added, their words are kept as their decision; do not add it again unless you find
new evidence, and then say so. When the person marks a relative as having died on their own word
(R-38), the kit treats that relative as dead. If you find a record of the death, add it as usual.

**Parents from a brother's or sister's records stay a possibility until the person says yes (BW-1).**
When a sibling's own records name parents for an ancestor whose parents are not known, you may
record that couple for the ancestor only as possible parents: `set_kind` `alternative_hypothesis`
with `set_kind_as_written` "from a sibling: ", citing the sibling's document as
indirect evidence about another person's line, at Weak or below. The helper refuses to make such
a set the main parents, or to let Quality Control pass its links, until the person says yes on
their Probable Pedigree page to the decision the program wrote for that very set (a yes to any
other decision, or to a proof of yours, does not count). A proof never retracts such a set,
changes its kind, moves its links or settles a fact taken from a sibling's record; families are
never merged so as to combine it with another set; and another set may use its links only on new
direct evidence from another record. Never give a placeholder parent ("not yet named") a name:
merge it into the real person instead.

Retract, never delete. Nothing is removed from the database: a wrong claim, document or link is
withdrawn with `retract` and a reason, and stays visible as withdrawn. Every change you make is
also logged in the tree itself, with your session, so the person can see it and undo it.

## 5. Evidence standards

MAXGEN's `confidence` number measures how faithfully a fact was read from its source —
extraction confidence — **not** how good the source is. A clearly printed name copied from a
clearly printed page is 0.9 even if the page is a hearsay family tree. How much the source is
worth is a separate question, answered for every MaxRecord by its `source_classification`, a
required field of the record:

- `source`: `original` (the document made at the time — a register page, a certificate, a
  stone — or an image of it), `derivative` (a copy, index, transcription or abstract made from
  an original; it must say what it was copied from, in `copied_from`), `authored` (someone's
  written conclusions — a compiled history, an online tree, the family's own account), or
  `undetermined` (only for a citation in an imported tree that nobody has examined yet).
- `information`: `primary` (the informant was present at the event), `secondary` (the
  informant heard it from someone else, or wrote it long afterwards), or `undetermined` (a
  census row, where nobody knows who answered the door). A record that holds several events
  judges this per event: a death certificate's informant is first-hand for the death and
  second-hand for the birth.

Every claim also says what kind of evidence it is: `direct` (the words state it), `indirect`
(it is worked out — a birth year from an age), or `negative` (someone missing from a complete
list).

These three sets of words follow the evidence analysis process map in Elizabeth Shown Mills's
*Evidence Explained*
([QuickLesson 17](https://www.evidenceexplained.com/content/quicklesson-17-evidence-analysis-process-map)),
described here in our own words.

A claim is called **proven** only when it meets the Genealogical Proof Standard (published by the
[Board for Certification of Genealogists](https://bcgcertification.org/ethics-standards/)) — a
reasonably exhaustive search, complete citations, analysis and correlation of the evidence,
resolution of any conflicts, and a written conclusion. In this kit that written conclusion is a
proof on a `resolve_conflict` task (or, for a merge, a `merge_person` task), and the status
"proven" is set only when the person accepts that proof on their own page ("Who decides",
above). Until then it is a claim with a confidence, and the kit says so. An import can mark a claim disputed or disproven, never proven.

## 6. The confidence score

`confidence` is a number from 0 to 1. It is how strongly *this document* supports *this claim*,
not how sure you feel. A census row names a person: 0.8 to 0.9. A gravestone with a worn date:
0.5 to 0.7. A family tree on a website with no citations: never above 0.4, and never alone.
It is extraction confidence; the weight of the evidence is the source classification above.

Deliberate exception, enforced by the helper: a claim whose evidence is not reliable — the
family's own account in the interview, something the person typed on their page, an online
tree, an imported file, a compiled work, a citation nobody has examined — is capped at 0.4 and
**never stands alone**: it never counts as independent evidence, never supports a proof, and
never shows that someone has died. Pages label it by where it came from ("From the family's
account", "From a family tree", "From an imported file", "Added by you"). The cap lifts only
when a new claim cites a reliable document.

Why this matters for AI: models that read handwriting, match records and draft leads need an honest confidence on every claim, a source they can be checked against, and the losing candidates as well as the winner. That is why every claim cites exactly one piece of evidence (for a document: the record, the line holding the words, the exact quote, and whether the evidence is direct, indirect or negative), why claims are never overwritten, and why a MaxTask can list the evidence its worker must hand back (addresses, exact queries, records saved) and its search log keeps every step, including the searches that found nothing.

## 7. Who may be living

Treat a person as possibly living unless at least one of these holds: a reliable document
states their death, burial or cremation (a later record calling their husband or wife a widow
or widower also counts; being missing from a list never does); their latest possible birth
year is 110 or more years ago; a marriage of theirs is 90 or more years ago; or a birth child
of theirs was born 90 or more years ago (always counting the latest year the date allows). A
step-child, ward, foster child or adopted child does not count. If none of these holds — for
example, when the birth year is unknown and no death is on file — assume living. Never infer
"deceased" from silence — not finding a death record is not a death record.

For those four rules only reliable evidence counts: a document classified `original` or
`derivative`, or a proof whose latest review is accepted. The family's own account, an online
tree, an imported file and a note typed on the person page do not show a death to them.

**R-40 (Probable Pedigree's helper, `DATES_A_ON`, on since 8 November 2026).** The helper's
living answer also counts recorded dates of any evidence but DNA, imported and unchecked ones
included: a death, burial or cremation that has a year in its date; a birth whose latest
possible year is 110 or more years ago; a marriage of theirs 90 or more years ago; or a birth
child of theirs (through a parent link that stands) whose latest possible birth year is 90 or
more years ago. (Probable Pedigree's sharing rule R-39 already lets a person with such a birth,
marriage or child be shared as having died; R-40 lets the living answer read the same dates.)
Any one of these shows the person as deceased and lets them be shared. A date kept as text only,
a claim worked out from absence, and anything resting on DNA never count. A marriage in a family
that Quality Control rejected (found false), or a child through a parent link it rejected, never
counts either. A stored `true` is a floor that beats the death-year, marriage and child clauses,
and a stored `false` is still never permission by itself. So a grandparent whose stored flag is
`false`, known only from the interview with a death year, is shown as deceased; one with no dates
stays living.

**R-40b (8 November 2026, the same switch).** The birth clause also beats a stored `true`: a
person whose recorded birth has a latest possible year 110 or more years ago, from any evidence
but DNA, imported and unchecked included, is shown as deceased even though the flag says living.
The order is: the person's own word that the relative died (R-38), then this birth clause, then
the stored `true` floor, then the four rules, the death year and the marriage and child clauses
as before. A birth that is only "before 1850" (the latest year is not known), births recorded as
both 1880 and 1990 (the latest is 1990) and a birth in 1963 leave a stored `true` standing, and
so does a death year, or a marriage or child 90 years ago, alone. The `tier2-private` licence
that every stored `true` carries is a lock of its own: it still keeps such a person out of a
shared copy until the flag and the licence are lowered with the person's yes. With `DATES_A_ON`
off the living answer is the four rules alone, as before R-40 (one fix stays in both modes: a
family or a parent link Quality Control rejected no longer counts for that sharing rule either).

**Common sense for R-40b (8 November 2026).** The birth clause does not beat a stored `true`
when the same person's other dated records show them alive more than 110 years after their
latest recorded birth year: a person recorded as born in 1891 who also has a census in 2020, a
marriage in 2005 or a child born in 2010 is not 135 years old; the year is most likely mistyped
(1891 for 1981), and the stored `true` stands. What counts is a dated record of any evidence but
DNA (imported and unchecked included; not a date kept as text only, nor one worked out from
absence): an event of theirs that needs them to be there (a census, a residence, a move, military
service, school, a job ending, a marriage or divorce) in a role other than father, mother, parent
or deceased, or their occupation, residence, education or military rank; a marriage or divorce
of a family of theirs that Quality Control has not rejected; or the birth of a child of theirs
through a parent link that stands. A burial, death, funeral, memorial, will, probate, estate
division, temple ordinance done for them after death (`lds_*`, `sealing`), pension, photograph or
adoption never counts, for such a record can be posthumous; nor does a date with an open start
("before 2005"). The guard keeps only a stored `true`: a person with no stored `true` and a birth
110 or more years ago is deceased by the birth clause whatever else is recorded.

Set `is_living` **explicitly** on every MaxPerson and every person named in a record, `true` or
`false`. The helper refuses a file that omits it. **The helper and every page work this out
again every time they read; a stored `false` never makes anyone shareable.** A stored `true` is
a floor: it stays until the person agrees to lower it (ORCHESTRATOR, "When the documents show
someone has died"). What the person tells you about living relatives stays `tier2-private` and
is used only for their own research — never published, exported or sent anywhere.

## 8. JSON examples

A MaxPerson is one person as a researched conclusion. Every fact about the person is a claim, kept in a list (the files name these lists `..._assertions`), and every claim cites exactly one piece of evidence and carries a confidence. A MaxPerson holds no family links: parents, children and partners live in MaxRelationship, where each link is stored once.

This made-up example takes three claims from one entry on a census page: a name, an occupation, and a birth year worked out from an age. The birth claim is `indirect` (the census gives an age, not a birth date), its date is marked `calculated` with a note saying how, and its confidence is lower than the others:

```json
{
  "person_id": "2a946e38-5769-5fdc-b888-e67cc4b40342",
  "schema_version": "2.0",
  "is_living": false,
  "redistribution_license": "CC0",
  "name_assertions": [
    {
      "name_as_written": "Mossbury, Amos",
      "given_name": "Amos",
      "surname": "Mossbury",
      "confidence": 0.9,
      "task_id": "f1f1f427-edc8-59ac-b068-c44d0daf5f82",
      "evidence": {
        "basis": "document",
        "source_record_id": "325d904c-1f07-52ff-85d2-856cb65a60cd",
        "mention_id": "11",
        "record_event_ref": "e1",
        "quote": "Mossbury, Amos",
        "kind": "direct"
      }
    }
  ],
  "birth_assertions": [
    {
      "date": {
        "modifier": "about",
        "value": {
          "year": 1896
        },
        "derivation": "calculated",
        "derivation_note": "age 44 on the 1940 census day"
      },
      "age_as_written": "44",
      "confidence": 0.6,
      "task_id": "f1f1f427-edc8-59ac-b068-c44d0daf5f82",
      "evidence": {
        "basis": "document",
        "source_record_id": "325d904c-1f07-52ff-85d2-856cb65a60cd",
        "mention_id": "11",
        "record_event_ref": "e1",
        "quote": "Mossbury, Amos | Head | M | 44",
        "kind": "indirect"
      }
    }
  ],
  "attribute_assertions": [
    {
      "attribute_type": "occupation",
      "value_as_written": "Miller",
      "occurrence_id": "8a37321b-3688-589b-8d1a-1a596a352edb",
      "confidence": 0.85,
      "task_id": "f1f1f427-edc8-59ac-b068-c44d0daf5f82",
      "evidence": {
        "basis": "document",
        "source_record_id": "325d904c-1f07-52ff-85d2-856cb65a60cd",
        "mention_id": "11",
        "record_event_ref": "e1",
        "quote": "Miller",
        "kind": "direct"
      }
    }
  ],
  "created_by_task_id": "f1f1f427-edc8-59ac-b068-c44d0daf5f82",
  "extensions": {
    "fixture": "made up"
  }
}
```

Paste any record into the [validator](/validator/) to check it, or press **Load a sample** there to see a made-up example of every kind.

### 8b. Contributor attribution

Credit travels with the data, not in a site footer. A MaxRecord can carry an `attribution{}` object crediting the human who photographed, transcribed or compiled it (`contributor_name`, `contributor_url`, `contributor_role`) and the organisation the document came from (`source_organization`, `source_organization_url`); a MaxSource and a MaxRecognition can carry one too. Every claim names the task that produced it (`task_id`), and each MaxTask records once, in its `provenance` block, who did the work: a person, an AI model (named), an OCR or handwriting reader, an importer, and so on. For a MaxRecognition, which holds one machine reading of an image, who or what made the reading is recorded the same way, on the task that produced it. A credit never makes a document count as naming a living person. In a copy meant for sharing, a credit is kept when it is already public or when the licence requires it (CC-BY, CC-BY-SA), exactly as the licence holder gave it; other credits, such as a name typed in as transcriber or photographer, are left out.

## 9. File format

A MAXGEN document is one JSON file of one kind: one MaxPerson, one MaxRecord, and so on. A document's kind is the first of these keys found at its top level: `dna_id`, `recognition_id`, `name_id`, `relationship_id`, `occurrence_id`, `place_id`, `group_id`, `record_id`, `task_id`, `source_id`, `person_id`. (MaxDNA also carries `person_id`, so the order matters.)

## 10. Versioning

All twelve files share one version number; the current release is v2.1. Every document carries a `schema_version` stamp. The schemas accept any `"2."` stamp (`"2.0"`, `"2.1"` and so on, but not `"1.13"`), and a file keeps the stamp it was written with.

**Within 2.x, every change is additive:** a new optional property, a new value in a list, a new shared definition in `maxgen-defs.schema.json`, a new record schema file, or a loosened limit. **Never:** removing or renaming a property, making an optional property required, narrowing a pattern, range or list, or changing what a value means. A file valid under 2.0 stays valid under every 2.x. Breaking changes wait for a new major version, with a new address space; the [governance page](/governance/) describes how changes are proposed and decided.

The 1.x files stay archived at `/schemas/maxgen/v1/`, with a frozen copy of every 1.x release, and their rules are unchanged. MAXGEN 2.0 does not read 1.x files, and there is no migration from 1.x to 2.0. Every release, with permanent download links, is on the [versions page](/versions/), and the full history is in the [changelog](/changelog/).

## 11. Why JSON?

- **Human-readable and machine-readable.** No proprietary parser required; you can open a record in a text editor.
- **Supported everywhere.** Every modern programming language reads and writes JSON natively.
- **Validated by JSON Schema 2020-12.** Structure is enforced at the moment a record is written, not discovered later.
- **Embeddable.** A MAXGEN record can be fed to an AI embedding model without conversion, which is what makes meaning-based search possible.
- **Version-control friendly.** Records can be diffed, reviewed and merged exactly like source code, so a community can review each other's work.
- **No lock-in.** Export your data at any time with zero loss.

## 12. How to contribute

Ask a question, report a problem, propose a change, or build something on the standard. You do not need permission for any of it. The [contribute page](/contribute/) has the details; the short version is: open a GitHub Issue using the *Schema Change Proposal* template (problem, proposed change, backward compatibility, examples) or write to maxgen@opengenealogyai.org.

## 13. Governance

MAXGEN is public domain, so anyone can use it, fork it, or extend it. What is stewarded is the canonical version: the one set of files at this address that may be called MAXGEN. Today the author, Garlon Maxwell, is the steward, with a public proposal process (7-day comment for minor changes, 30-day for major) and written decisions. A published charter describes the advisory board that takes over major-version decisions once there are independent adopters, including how it can overrule the steward. What the steward never controls: your forks, your extensions, your tools, or your records. Read the full [governance page](/governance/).

> "MAXGEN is open because anyone can use it and build on it. It is not open to fragmentation. One canonical version. One steward. Every change earns its place in the record." — Garlon Maxwell


---
## The MAXGEN schemas

MAXGEN v2.1 · twelve files, one version
# The schemas

Since version 2.0, MAXGEN has eleven record schemas plus one shared building-blocks file; the current release is 2.1. Every file is JSON Schema Draft 2020-12. All twelve files share one version number, and within 2.x every change is additive: a file valid under 2.0 stays valid under every 2.x.



## Shared building blocks

`maxgen-defs.schema.json` is not a record type: no document is valid against it alone. It holds the parts every record schema uses: ids and small types, the date block, the place block, the evidence link (the part of every claim that says which evidence it rests on), the quote check, saved copies, regions and media pointers, roles and event types, the claim header, the common and lifecycle fields, and the task provenance block. [Download the shared file](/schemas/maxgen/v2/maxgen-defs.schema.json).

## Canonical addresses



Every file declares its own address in its `$id`. A record schema points into the shared file by a relative address, so all twelve files sit side by side in one folder. Validators load all twelve files into one registry and never fetch anything over the network; the addresses do not need to be reachable for validation to work. The fingerprints are also in [SHA256SUMS.txt](/schemas/maxgen/v2/SHA256SUMS.txt), and a machine-readable list of every version is at [`/schemas/maxgen/index.json`](/schemas/maxgen/index.json).

## MAXGEN 1.13 (archived) {#archived-113}

The seven 1.13 schema files stay exactly as they were, at their permanent addresses under `/schemas/maxgen/v1/` and `/schemas/maxgen/v1.NN/`. MAXGEN 2.0 does not read 1.x files. The 1.13 pages are kept for reference: .

## Check a record

Paste any JSON record into the [browser validator](/validator/) to see whether it conforms. Nothing you paste leaves your computer.

## FAQ

Questions and answers
# Frequently asked questions

Grouped by who is asking. If your question is not here, [ask it](/contribute/) and it may be added.

## I'm a genealogist

What is MAXGEN in one sentence?A free, public-domain way of writing down family-history evidence so that every fact keeps its source and an honest confidence score, and conflicting evidence is kept rather than deleted.

Do I need to be technical to benefit from it?No. MAXGEN is what software uses underneath. What you notice is the behaviour: a tree that keeps two possible fathers, each with its evidence, instead of silently picking one, a search that finds "Quilfether" when you typed "Quillfeather", and a document that is never "corrected" away from what the clerk wrote.

Why keep several possible parents? Isn't the job to find the right one?Yes, and keeping the candidates is how you get there honestly. Real research often ends at "probably this man, possibly that one". A format that can hold only one answer has no room for the uncertainty a good genealogist would write in the margin. MAXGEN stores the margin note as data: a competing set of parents is kept as its own link, with its own evidence, marked as not yet settled until a written proof settles it, so a new record adds evidence instead of overturning a false certainty.

What do the confidence numbers mean?A confidence is a number from 0 to 1. It is how strongly this document supports this claim, not how sure you feel. A census row names a person: 0.8 to 0.9. A gravestone with a worn date: 0.5 to 0.7. A family tree on a website with no citations: never above 0.4, and never alone. It measures how faithfully a fact was read from its source; how much the source itself is worth is recorded separately, on the document, as its source classification. A claim whose evidence is not reliable (the family's own account, an online tree, an imported file) is capped at 0.4 and never counts as independent evidence. The full rule is on the standard page.

How does it handle a document that gets the spelling wrong?The document record (MaxRecord) keeps the spelling exactly as written. The interpretation ("that is the Quillfeather family") lives separately, as a claim with its own evidence and confidence. And the name record (MaxName) can state, citing evidence, that Quilfether is a spelling variant of Quillfeather used between 1700 and 1800, so searches find it.

Will my existing GEDCOM files work?MAXGEN is not a replacement for GEDCOM as a way to move a finished tree between programs. It is a way to exchange the evidence and reasoning behind a tree. MAXGEN 2.0 gives every GEDCOM 7 construct a place to land, so a tool that brings your file into MAXGEN need not lose anything: each fact arrives as a claim that remembers it came from your tree, and it serves as a lead (with a confidence of at most 0.4) until a document confirms it.

What about living relatives?Every document that names a person must say whether that person may be alive; a document that leaves it out is refused, and when in doubt the answer is "living". Anything about a person who may be alive is tier2-private (kept private), and whether someone may be living is worked out again whenever the data is read, so a stored "no" never makes anyone shareable. DNA records are always private and can never hold raw genetic data. Research tasks about living people must stay first-party: they can never be opened to outside contributors. These are rules of the standard, not settings an application can turn off.

Can AI make things up in a MAXGEN record?It can try, and the standard is built to catch it. Every claim must cite exactly one piece of evidence; a claim drawn from a document names the line it comes from and quotes the exact words (or marks the area of the image), and quotes are checked against the document's words. A research task can list the evidence its worker must hand back (addresses, exact queries, records saved), and its search log keeps every step, including the searches that found nothing. Reviews are separate tasks that are never overwritten, "fabricated or hallucinated" is a formal rejection reason, and in 2.0 nothing can be marked proven without a human's review of a written proof.

Does it cost anything?No. The standard is dedicated to the public domain (CC0): use it for anything, including commercial products, with no conditions. The schemas, the specification, and the podcasts on this site cost nothing.

## I'm a developer

What format is it?JSON, described by JSON Schema (draft 2020-12). Twelve schema files, all at the same version number: eleven record schemas, one for each kind of document, and one shared building-blocks file (maxgen-defs.schema.json) that the others point into. Each document is a plain JSON file of one kind; its kind is told by the first id key found at its top level (dna_id, recognition_id, name_id and so on, with person_id last).

Where do I get the schema files?At their canonical addresses, which are also each file's $id: https://opengenealogyai.org/schemas/maxgen/v2/&lt;file name&gt;, for example .../v2/person.schema.json. A frozen copy of the 2.0 release lives under /schemas/maxgen/v2.0/, with a SHA-256 list, and the archived 1.x files stay at /schemas/maxgen/v1/ and /schemas/maxgen/v1.NN/. Validators load all twelve files locally and never need to fetch an address over the network. See the schemas page and versions.

How do I validate a record?With any JSON Schema 2020-12 validator that can hold several schema files in one registry. Load all twelve files (the shared maxgen-defs.schema.json first) and do not let the validator fetch anything over the network. In Python that is jsonschema 4.18 or later with referencing; in JavaScript it is Ajv 2020, calling ajv.addSchema() with the shared file before compiling a record schema. The schema repository ships validators and made-up fixtures. Or paste a record into the browser validator on this site.

Can I add my own fields?Yes, in extensions{}, which every record schema has (claims, mentions and other smaller items have one too) and which accepts anything. Apart from a few named places, every other object is closed: unknown field names are refused, so validation is exact, and the extensions object is open so you never need to fork. Your records stay valid across 2.x releases.

Will an update break my records?Not within 2.x. Every change inside 2.x is additive: a new optional property, a new value in a list, a new shared definition, a new record schema file, or a loosened limit. Properties are never removed or renamed, optional ones never become required, patterns, ranges and lists are never narrowed, and what a value means never changes, so a file valid under 2.0 stays valid under every 2.x. The step from 1.x to 2.0 was different: it was a breaking change, 2.0 does not read 1.x files, and there is no migration. The 1.x files stay archived at their /v1/ addresses with their rules unchanged. See the changelog.

Why is one version number shared by all twelve files?So there is never any doubt about which files go together: you adopt MAXGEN 2.x as a set. Every document carries a schema_version stamp, and the schemas accept any 2.x stamp, so a file keeps the stamp it was written with. From v1.3 to v1.13 every release re-stamped all seven files, even those that did not change; 2.x drops that ritual. Before v1.3 the schemas versioned independently, and the skew was confusing.

Which fields are required?Few, deliberately, and each kind has its own. Every document needs its own id (person_id, record_id and so on) and schema_version, and every claim needs evidence and a confidence. Beyond that: a MaxPerson needs is_living, redistribution_license and at least one name claim (a placeholder person needs a placeholder_label instead); a MaxRecord needs record_type, redistribution_license, is_living_flag, source_classification and a way to find the document (a source_url, a saved copy, or a repository or source with a locator); a MaxRelationship needs kind, is_living_flag and redistribution_license, plus what its kind needs (a parent-child pair names the parent and the child); a MaxTask needs task_type, status and is_living_flag; a MaxSource needs name, source_type, redistribution_license and is_living_flag; a MaxPlace needs redistribution_license and at least one name claim; a MaxGroup needs group_kind, is_living_flag, redistribution_license and at least one name claim; a MaxEvent needs event_type, origin, is_living_flag and redistribution_license; a MaxName needs canonical_form, name_type and redistribution_license; a MaxRecognition needs recognition_type, output_text, processed_at, is_living_flag, redistribution_license and an image_url or raw_record_id; a MaxDNA needs person_id, test_type, kit_source, is_living_flag, redistribution_license, raw_genotype_stored and consent_status, and a kit_id_hash unless kit_id_status is unknown. Each schema page lists its fields with the required ones marked.

What are the normative rules I must implement?The privacy rules are written into the schemas, so every valid document already obeys them. Every document that names a person must say whether that person may be alive (is_living on a MaxPerson and on each person a record names, is_living_flag on the other kinds that can name someone), and anything that may concern a living person must be tier2-private. A MaxDNA document is always tier2-private, raw_genotype_stored is always false, and no raw kit number is ever stored, only a keyed fingerprint. A saved DNA match list is always treated as living and private. A MaxTask about someone who may be living must keep contributor_eligibility at first_party_only. Two rules no schema can check complete the core: when unsure, a person counts as living, and whether someone may be living is worked out again every time the data is read, so a stored false is never permission to share. Rules a schema cannot express are stated in the field descriptions.

How are confidence scores combined?They are not stored combined. Each claim keeps its own confidence, and no schema has a field for a computed score: anything worked out from the evidence, such as whether two sources are independent, is worked out when the data is read. Independence fails closed: two documents count as independent only when they are different originals with different informants, and a claim whose evidence is not reliable (an online tree, an imported file, the family's own account) never counts toward it. That is how one document copied twice is never counted twice.

Is there an official library or package?Not yet. The schema repository contains JavaScript validators and made-up fixtures. Packages for npm and PyPI are planned after launch; if you publish one, tell us and it will be listed.

How do I propose a change?Open a GitHub Issue with the problem, the proposed fields, the backward-compatibility answer and a before-and-after example. Minor changes get at least a week of open discussion, major ones a month, then a written decision. Details on the governance page.

## I run an archive, library or society

What would adopting MAXGEN commit us to?Only to publishing records that validate against the public schemas and to honouring the privacy rules they carry. There is no membership, no fee, no agreement to sign, and no obligation to use the whole standard: an archive that only wants to publish its documents, copied word for word, can start with MaxRecord alone (plus the shared building-blocks file every schema uses).

Who owns the standard?Nobody, legally: it is dedicated to the public domain under CC0, so anyone may use, copy, change and redistribute it with no conditions. The canonical version is stewarded by its author today, with a published path to an advisory board that includes an archive or library seat and can overrule the steward on major versions by a two-thirds vote. See governance.

Can we keep our own catalogue numbers and internal fields?Yes. A MaxRecord says where the item sits in your own words (repository_as_written, collection_as_written) and in a structured locator (volume, page, line and so on), and extensions{} holds anything else. A MaxSource for a collection lists the repositories that hold it, with their call numbers and which one holds the original (holdings), and its access block records how you want to be reached, including politeness and rate-limit notes for automated searching.

How does it handle attribution and licensing of our records?Every record declares its own licence: CC0, public-domain, CC-BY, CC-BY-SA, all_rights_reserved, or tier2-private (kept private). A record can also carry an attribution{} object for the credit line your licence requires, and when a licence requires credit, a copy made for sharing keeps it exactly as you gave it. The standard itself is public domain; your data stays under whatever terms you set.

We have transcriptions made by volunteers over decades. Is that work preserved?Yes. A volunteer's transcription is kept as a MaxRecord: the words exactly as transcribed, classified as a derivative (a copy made from an original) that says what it was copied from, with the volunteer credited by name and role (transcriber, indexer, translator and so on) in its attribution{}. Machine readings (OCR of print, HTR of handwriting) get a MaxRecognition, which can keep a confidence for every word and note which words were read from the image and which were inferred. Either way the work becomes citable instead of being flattened into a text field.

## About the project

Why is it called MAXGEN?It stands for the Maxwell Genealogy Standard, after its author Garlon Maxwell. The name is a mark for the canonical version: use it for anything that validates against the public schemas, but not for a fork that diverges.

What is OpenGenealogyAI, and what is The Probable Pedigree?OpenGenealogyAI is the organisation that stewards MAXGEN. The Probable Pedigree is a genealogy platform built on the standard that shows what it makes possible. The standard is designed to outlive any product, including that one: it has no special standing in the change process.

Why eleven schemas instead of one?Because documents, people, family links, work, sources, places, groups, occasions, names, machine readings and DNA are different things with different privacy needs. Separating them lets a document be re-read without touching conclusions, lets each family link be stored once instead of on both people, lets one place, group or occasion be described once and pointed at by many claims, and lets DNA be locked down harder than everything else.

Who made the podcasts?They were produced with an AI narration tool from scripts written by the standard's author, and they describe MAXGEN v1.11, when there were seven schemas. Much has changed since then: the schema pages and the changelog on this site are authoritative.

How does this relate to FamilySearch, Ancestry, WikiTree and the other sites?They hold the records and the communities; MAXGEN is a format for describing evidence that any of them, and any tool built around them, could read and write. It is not a competing service and it does not replace anyone's database. A MaxPerson can record, with evidence and a confidence, that it is the same person as a profile on FamilySearch, WikiTree or Find a Grave, so research done in different places can be reconciled instead of duplicated. The aim is a shared language, and the more sites speak it the more useful everyone's work becomes.

Is MAXGEN trying to replace GEDCOM?No. GEDCOM moves finished trees between programs and has done so for forty years. MAXGEN carries the evidence and reasoning behind a tree, which GEDCOM was never designed to hold. MAXGEN 2.0 gives every GEDCOM 7 construct a home, and a tool can happily support both.

How do I follow changes?Every release is recorded in the changelog with the reason it happened. Proposals are discussed in public on GitHub. A mailing list is planned.

## Versions

Releases · current v2.1
# Versions and the stability promise

## How versions work

**One version number for all twelve files.** The eleven record schemas and the shared building-blocks file are released together as one MAXGEN version, so you adopt "MAXGEN 2.1" as a set and never have to wonder which file goes with which. Every document carries `schema_version`, and the 2.x schemas accept any `"2."` stamp (`"2.0"`, `"2.1"` and so on; not `"2.01"`, not `"1.13"`).

## The 2.x promise

> **Within 2.x, every change is additive:** a new optional property, a new value in a list, a new shared definition in `maxgen-defs.schema.json` (a `$defs` entry), a new record schema file, or a loosened limit. **Never:** removing or renaming a property, making an optional property required, narrowing a pattern, range or list, or changing what a value means. A file valid under 2.0 stays valid under every 2.x.

- **Files keep the stamp they were written with.** There is no re-stamping of old files at each release.
- **Unknown values fall back safely.** A reader that meets a list value it does not know reads a vocabulary word as `other` and shows the words as written; a state that software manages fails closed (an unknown licence is read as `tier2-private`).
- **A major version** (`v2` → `v3`) means breaking changes and a new `$id` address space.

## What 2.0 changed

MAXGEN 2.0 is the first major version. It reshaped the seven 1.x schemas, added four new ones (MaxRelationship, MaxPlace, MaxGroup and MaxEvent) and a shared building-blocks file, and moved family links out of MaxPerson into MaxRelationship, where each link is stored once. **2.0 does not read 1.x files, and there is no migration from 1.x.** The 1.x files are not deleted: they stay at their permanent addresses, unchanged. The [changelog](/changelog/#v20-2026-10-16) lists what changed in every schema and what breaks.

## What 2.1 added

MAXGEN 2.1 adds optional fields and allowed values to six of the twelve files: where a fact came from, life stories and biographies, notes that keep their history, comparing a reading with an index, health conditions kept private, archive addresses and old-map alignment. Nothing was removed or narrowed, so every 2.0 file stays valid. The [changelog](/changelog/#v21-2026-11-21) lists every addition in the schema files' own words.

2.0 and 2.1 were published without the public comment period described on the [governance page](/governance/), because the standard had no outside users yet.

## Permanent addresses

- `/schemas/maxgen/v2/` holds the **current 2.x files** (now 2.1). This is the `$id` inside every 2.x file.
- `/schemas/maxgen/v2.1/` and `/schemas/maxgen/v2.0/` are **frozen copies** of each release.
- `/schemas/maxgen/v1/.schema.json` and `/schemas/maxgen/v1.NN/.schema.json` hold the **archived 1.x releases**, unchanged.
- `/schemas/maxgen/index.json` lists every version, with each 2.x file's SHA-256, for machines.



## Changelog

Every release, what changed in each schema and why, is on the [changelog page](/changelog/).

## Governance

How the standard changes
# Governance

MAXGEN is dedicated to the public domain (CC0). Anyone can use it, fork it, extend it, or build on it without asking. What is stewarded is the **canonical version**: the one set of files at `opengenealogyai.org/schemas/maxgen/` that may be called MAXGEN. This page says who decides what goes into it, how, and how that will change as the community grows.

> "MAXGEN is open because anyone can use it and build on it. It is not open to fragmentation. One canonical version. One steward. Every change earns its place in the record." — Garlon Maxwell

## Today: a steward

The standard's author, Garlon Maxwell, is the steward: the technical lead who has final say on what enters the canonical schemas until the advisory board exists. Every decision is public, reasoned, and recorded in the [changelog](/changelog/). This is the same arrangement most successful standards began with, including the OpenAPI specification before it moved to a foundation, and the page below says exactly when and how it ends.

## How to propose a change

1. **Open a GitHub Issue** in the schema repository using the *Schema Change Proposal* template. It asks four things:
    - **Problem**: what real use the current schema fails to support.
    - **Proposed change**: the new or altered fields, with type and description.
    - **Backward compatibility**: does any existing valid record become invalid? If so, how would it migrate?
    - **Examples**: at least one before-and-after JSON snippet.
2. **Open discussion.** Anyone may comment. Minor (additive) changes stay open at least **7 days**; major (breaking) changes at least **30 days**.
3. **Review.** The steward reads the proposal and the discussion, may ask for more examples, and may put the question to a wider vote.
4. **Decision with reasons.** Accepted or declined, in writing, on the issue. Nothing merges without explicit sign-off.
5. **Implementation.** The change is applied to the schema files, fixtures are re-validated, the changelog is written, and a new version is released under the [versioning policy](/versions/).

Challenges that did **not** lead to a change are logged too. A rule that survived a good argument is worth knowing about.

If you do not use GitHub, write to **maxgen@opengenealogyai.org** and the steward will open the issue on your behalf.

## Tomorrow: an advisory board

A standard controlled by one person is a standard institutions hesitate to adopt. The path to shared control is published now so that adopters can see it.

**Trigger.** The board convenes when there are three or more independent implementations of MAXGEN, or when the first institution (an archive, a library, a genealogical society, a software vendor) adopts it, whichever comes first.

**Composition.** Five to seven seats: the steward, working genealogists, developers who have shipped an implementation, and at least one representative of an archive or library. No single company may hold a majority.

**What the board decides.** Major versions, additions to the core schemas, and changes to the normative privacy rules. Extensions need nobody's permission and are never voted on.

**What the steward keeps.** A tie-breaking vote and custody of the name and the canonical address. The steward may be **overruled on a major version by a two-thirds vote**. That clause is the point: it is the guarantee that the standard cannot be held hostage by its author.

**Openness.** Meetings are announced in advance, minutes are published on this site, and every vote is recorded.

**How seats are filled.** The first board is appointed by the steward from people who have actually implemented or adopted MAXGEN, announced publicly with a 30-day objection period. After that, seats are two-year terms; the sitting board fills vacancies by simple majority from public nominations. Anyone may nominate anyone, including themselves.

**Quorum and voting.** A quorum is a majority of seats. Additive changes pass by simple majority of those voting. Major versions and changes to the privacy rules need two-thirds of all seats. Every vote is recorded with names.

**Emergency fixes.** A security or privacy defect in a schema may be patched immediately by the steward as a patch release, with a public notice the same day and retrospective board review within 30 days. Nothing else skips the process.

## Continuity: what happens if the steward is gone

A standard that dies with one person is not a standard. Three safeguards:

1. **The licence is CC0.** Nobody needs permission to carry on. If the canonical site went dark, every schema file and this whole site could be republished by anyone, from the public git history, the same day.
2. **A named successor.** The steward keeps a named successor on file with the board (or, before the board exists, publicly in the repository). If the steward is unreachable for 90 days, the successor, or the board by majority, assumes stewardship and the name.
3. **Frozen releases.** Every version is archived at a permanent address, so an adopter never depends on the steward being available to fetch the files they validated against.

## What the steward does not control

- Private forks and extensions. Add fields in `extensions{}` or fork the files outright. No permission needed.
- Tools built on MAXGEN. Commercial or free, open or closed.
- Records you publish in MAXGEN format.
- Proposals. All are welcome and all get an answer.

What you may not do is call a diverging fork "MAXGEN". The name means the canonical version.

## Conflict of interest

The steward's own genealogy platform, The Probable Pedigree, implements MAXGEN. It gets no special treatment: its change requests go through the same public process, and anything specific to its business (pricing, payments, accounts) stays in `extensions{}` and never enters the standard. The MaxTask schema deliberately contains no payment fields for exactly this reason.

## Contribute

Get involved
# Contribute

## Ask a question

- **GitHub Discussions** on the [OpenGenealogyAI organisation](https://github.com/OpenGenealogyai): free to read, free account to post. Questions that keep coming up are promoted into the [FAQ](/faq/).
- **Email**: maxgen@opengenealogyai.org, for anyone who would rather not use GitHub.

## Report a problem

Found a record that should validate but does not, a description that contradicts the field, or a fixture that is wrong? Open an issue in the schema repository with the JSON that shows it. A reproducible example is worth more than a paragraph.

## Propose a change

Follow the process on the [governance page](/governance/): problem, proposed change, backward compatibility, examples. Additive proposals that come with a fixture are the easiest to accept.

## Build on it

You do not need permission. Some useful starting points:

- Validate records against the canonical schemas at `https://opengenealogyai.org/schemas/maxgen/v2/` (load all twelve files, the shared `maxgen-defs.schema.json` first), or try the [browser validator](/validator/).
- Keep your own fields in `extensions{}` so your records stay valid across 2.x releases.
- Honour the privacy rules the schemas carry: every document that names a person says whether that person may be alive, and anyone who may be alive stays private (`tier2-private`); DNA stays private and never holds raw genotypes; and tasks about living people are never opened to outside contributors.
- Tell us. Implementations are listed on this site, and three independent ones convene the advisory board.

## Help with the content

The FAQ and the schema pages are all improvable. Corrections and clearer wording are welcome as issues or pull requests against the website repository.

## Licence

# Licence

## The standard: CC0

The MAXGEN schema files (the twelve files of MAXGEN 2.x and every archived 1.x file) and the text of the standard on this site are dedicated to the public domain under the [Creative Commons CC0 1.0 Universal](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/) dedication. You may copy, change, redistribute and build on them for any purpose, commercial or not, without asking and without attribution.

Why CC0 rather than a licence that requires credit? Because a standard only works when adopting it costs nothing, legally or administratively. An archive's counsel should be able to approve MAXGEN in one reading. Credit is welcome, never required.

### If you want to credit us anyway

- In software or documentation: *"Uses the MAXGEN standard by OpenGenealogyAI (opengenealogyai.org)."*
- In a dataset: every MAXGEN document already carries its `schema_version`, and the schema files it validates against carry their `opengenealogyai.org` address in their `$id`.
- In a paper or article: cite as shown at the bottom of this page.

## Records: each carries its own

Every MAXGEN document except a MaxTask (a record of work, which has no licence field) declares its own `redistribution_license`: `CC0`, `public-domain`, `CC-BY`, `CC-BY-SA`, `all_rights_reserved`, or `tier2-private` (keep it private). Where a source requires attribution, the `attribution{}` object in the record holds the credit. The standard is public domain; the data written in it is whatever its owner says it is.

## Code: MIT

The validators, fixtures and tooling in the schema repository are released under the [MIT licence](https://opensource.org/license/mit).

## Names and logo

"MAXGEN", "OpenGenealogyAI" and the star-tree logo identify the canonical standard and its steward. Use them to say your software implements MAXGEN. Do not use them for a fork that diverges from the canonical schemas, and do not imply that OpenGenealogyAI endorses your product unless it does.

## How to cite

> Maxwell, G. *MAXGEN: The Maxwell Genealogy Standard*, version 2.1. OpenGenealogyAI. https://opengenealogyai.org/ — CC0 1.0.

## Podcasts

Listen · eight episodes · about 20 minutes each
# The MAXGEN podcast

Each of the seven original schemas gets one conversation. Start with the overview if you are new, or jump to the schema you care about.

Subscribe in any podcast app with the feed address **`https://opengenealogyai.org/podcasts/feed.xml`**.

These episodes were produced with an AI narration tool from written scripts by the standard's author, and describe MAXGEN v1.11. MAXGEN 2.0 changed a great deal since, so each episode links to what changed. Where an episode and a schema page disagree, the schema page is authoritative. The four schemas new in 2.0 (MaxRelationship, MaxPlace, MaxGroup and MaxEvent) have no episode yet.


---
## MaxRecord (MAXGEN 2.1 schema)

Page: https://opengenealogyai.org/schemas/maxrecord/
File: https://opengenealogyai.org/schemas/maxgen/v2/raw-record.schema.json  SHA-256 ad38d5a1d421bcd74389c2bddb6887d62a2c66ac88cf092f9af3e0d8d502bd67
One MaxRecord is one document, copied word for word.

Definition: MAXGEN 2.0 -- One MaxRecord is one original document (or one copy of it), copied word for word with every person it names and every event it records, so that one original equals one record.

### Fields

- record_id (uuid, required): This record's permanent random id, created once by the writer and never recomputed or reused.
- record_type (enum, required): What kind of document this is; census_household holds a whole household, gazetteer_entry is an authored gazetteer or authority page, and dna_match_list is always tier2-private and living.
- record_type_as_written (string): The document's or program's own words for its type, used with other.
- redistribution_license (licence, required): Whether this record may be shared, and under what licence; must be tier2-private while is_living_flag is true.
- is_living_flag (boolean, required): Living A: whether anyone this record names may be alive (unsure means true); true requires tier2-private, it is a floor that only rises, and privacy is always worked out again when read.
- source_classification (source_classification, required): Whether the document is an original, a copy or an authored work, and how first-hand its information is overall.
- transcription_parts (array of transcription_part): The document's text word for word, in labelled parts; a line that starts with [label] and one space carries that line label.
- transcription_scope (enum): How much of the document was transcribed; only complete_entry or complete_list can carry evidence of absence; required when transcription_parts is present.
- transcription_sha256 (sha256): Helper-owned fingerprint of transcription_parts in canonical form, used to tell when quote checks are stale.
- extraction_confidence (confidence): How faithfully the transcription follows the document, from 0 to 1; required when transcription_parts is present.
- persons_mentioned (array of mention): Every person the document names, one mention each, as written.
- events_documented (array of event_entry): The events this document records, one entry each (one per child for twins); the helper gives each entry its own occurrence.
- record_date (date): The date the entry or document was written, not the date of the event it records.
- record_place (place_ref): Where the document was made, as written.
- record_status (enum): Whether this is the first issue of the document or an amended, delayed or reissued one; lineage facts citing an amended, delayed or reissued record are flagged for review (R-18).
- record_status_as_written (string): The document's own words for its status, used with other.
- copied_from (array of copy_step): The step back toward the original that this copy was made from; required with at least one step when the source is derivative, and the full chain is found by following record ids, never copied here.
- part_of_source_id (uuid): The MaxSource (collection, book, film) this record belongs to; containment, kept apart from copying.
- repository_as_written (string): The archive, library or family holding the document, as written.
- collection_as_written (string): The collection the document sits in, as written.
- locator (locator): Where the document sits in its collection: volume, page, line and so on.
- original_key (original_key): Helper-built stable name of the original document, used to refuse duplicates and to judge independence; never written by hand.
- source_url (uri): The web address where the document was read; optional, and never invented.
- citation_as_written (string): A footnote or citation string exactly as another program or publication gave it.
- citation_template (citation_template): A citation template another program used for this document, with its field values.
- saved_copies (array of saved_copy): The files this record captured, each described here once and keyed by fingerprint; frozen once stored apart from their descriptive fields.
- media_refs (array of media_ref): Files described on another record that this record also uses.
- attribution (attribution): Credit for the human who photographed, transcribed or compiled this record; a credit never sets a living flag.
- rights_uri (uri): A web address stating the rights in this document.
- sensitive_data_redacted (boolean): True when sensitive details (identity numbers, medical details) were left out of the transcription.
- redaction_notes (string): What was left out and why.
- archive_ref (string): A local path where this record is kept; private, never exported.
- cited_record_ids (array of uuid): MAXGEN 2.1 (G-29): on a life_story record only, the documents the story draws on; each must exist (R-04), as MaxPlace lists its own.

### Example (made up; marriage_register_1880_obadiah_patience.json)

```json
{
  "record_id": "71642fb1-7db2-5581-8a08-cb4df77ea03e",
  "schema_version": "2.0",
  "record_type": "marriage_register",
  "redistribution_license": "public-domain",
  "is_living_flag": false,
  "source_classification": {
    "source": "original",
    "information": "primary"
  },
  "transcription_parts": [
    {
      "part_id": "p1",
      "lang": "en",
      "text": "[4] 1 May 1880 | Obadiah Mossbury, bachelor | Patience Wren, spinster"
    }
  ],
  "transcription_scope": "complete_entry",
  "extraction_confidence": 0.95,
  "persons_mentioned": [
    {
      "mention_id": "m1",
      "name_as_written": "Obadiah Mossbury",
      "role_as_written": "groom",
      "role": "groom",
      "in_event_refs": [
        "e1"
      ],
      "lines": [
        "4"
      ],
      "is_living": false
    },
    {
      "mention_id": "m2",
      "name_as_written": "Patience Wren",
      "role_as_written": "bride",
      "role": "bride",
      "in_event_refs": [
        "e1"
      ],
      "lines": [
        "4"
      ],
      "is_living": false
    }
  ],
  "events_documented": [
    {
      "ref": "e1",
      "event_type": "marriage",
      "is_primary": true,
      "date": {
        "value": {
          "year": 1880,
          "month": 5,
          "day": 1
        },
        "as_written": "1 May 1880"
      },
      "place": {
        "place_as_written": "St Wren's, Tumblebrook"
      },
      "information": "primary"
    }
  ],
  "part_of_source_id": "75df6185-5f2f-5652-afb4-fb6349ea015f",
  "locator": {
    "as_written": "Tumblebrook marriages, entry 4",
    "register": "marriages",
    "entry": "4"
  },
  "created_by_task_id": "f29d3707-1833-510d-ae04-a2304e60a471",
  "extensions": {
    "fixture": "made up"
  }
}
```

### What changed from 1.13

One original, one record, holding the whole entry. `transcription` becomes
`transcription_parts` with permanent line labels, `transcription_scope` (complete entry,
complete list, partial) and a kit-computed fingerprint. Added: `persons_mentioned` with a
permanent `mention_id`, the page's own role words and `is_living` for every person;
`events_documented`, the events the document records, each with `information` judged per event
(each gets an occasion id); `source_classification` as a required core field (it was under
`extensions`); `copied_from` (the copying chain, required for a derivative); `part_of_source_id`
and `locator`; a kit-built `original_key` that refuses a second copy of the same original;
`record_status` (amended, delayed, reissued); `saved_copies` and `media_refs`;
`citation_as_written` and `citation_template`. `source_url` becomes optional, but "where it is"
is required (an address, a saved copy, or a repository or source with a locator; never an
invented URL). `record_date` is the date the entry was written. `census_row` is renamed
`census_household`; new types include `birth_register`, `death_register`, `tree_import`,
`gazetteer_entry` and `dna_match_list`. Removed: `transcription`, `image_url`, `locations`,
`repository`, `collection` (now `_as_written` fields), `language`, `alternate_names`,
`digital_object_id`, `extracted_by`, `extracted_at`.

### Added in 2.1

- cited_record_ids (new field): MAXGEN 2.1 (G-29): on a life_story record only, the documents the story draws on; each must exist (R-04), as MaxPlace lists its own.
- record_type: new allowed value life_story

### Listen

Episode 1, MaxRecord — Source documents as written (25:40): https://opengenealogyai.org/podcasts/audio/MAXGEN-01-maxrecord.mp3 — Evidence versus interpretation, and why the clerk who wrote 'Makeswell' must never be corrected. It describes MAXGEN v1.11; see https://opengenealogyai.org/changelog/#v20-2026-10-16 for what changed since.
